short: Moves online large-vocabulary decoding to 2.5% WER and 248 h of home use; rapid calibration is a cross-study claim and the 97.5% conversation accuracy matches the Copy Task figure.
position: The paper changes calibration data (M03), array placement (M05) and sustained home use (M13); each is standard by the verdict rules (one participant, no within-participant ablation), yet together they move online large-vocabulary decoding from 23.8% WER [@willett2023] to 2.5% in the final Copy Task sessions, the lowest online large-vocabulary WER among the topic's ledger candidates (Appendix). Rapid calibration holds as a description, 9.8% WER on 125,000 words after about 473 prompted sentences, comparable to one day of T12's calibration sentences (inference), but not as a property of the method: the T12 comparison crosses participants, placements and language models. The strongest overreach is the abstract's 97.5% accuracy for conversations, which equals 100 minus the Copy Task WER of 2.5% (inference); measured conversational WER is 3.7% in selected sessions, against references partly reconstructed by asking the participant afterwards. Home use over 8.4 months is the real advance; other users remain untested, as the authors concede.
